findings.text: The variable-ratio schedule's resistance to extinction is one of the reasons the text gives for gambling being so addictive.
findings.problem: Inverts the source's causal structure. The source gives the variable-ratio schedule (people keep trying because they never know when the next win comes) as one reason gambling is so addictive AND so resistant to extinction; it does not give resistance to extinction as the reason for addictiveness.
findings.evidence: converted L11476-11479: 'Because the reinforcement schedule in most types of gambling has a variable ratio schedule, people keep trying and hoping that the next time they will win big. This is one of the reasons that gambling is so addictive—and so resistant to extinction.'
findings.fix: correct: The text gives the variable-ratio schedule of most gambling as one of the reasons gambling is so addictive and so resistant to extinction.

findings.text: WEIRD stands for western, educated, industrialised, rich, and democratic; the differences between WEIRD and other societies show up in perception, cooperation, and moral reasoning [AP] (Ch 1.2, "Multicultural and Cross-Cultural Psychology").
findings.problem: The differences in perception, cooperation and moral reasoning are Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan's findings relayed by the text, so the marker should be [BT], not [AP]. The [V] quotation in the preceding sentence is verbatim and the locator is correct.
findings.evidence: converted L1361-1364: 'Henrich, Heine, and Norenzayan found that there are many differences between people in the WEIRD group and people in less industrialized, less urban, and nonWestern societies. These differences occur in a variety of areas, including perception, cooperation, and moral reasoning.'

findings.text: LFUO's procedural responses (interview as soon as possible, Handout C; avoid counterfactual arguments such as "but we should have known...", Part 9) are the direct counters.
findings.problem: The example utterance 'but we should have known...' now sits inside the LFUO attribution with a Part 9 locator, so it reads as LFUO's own example. LFUO's Part 9 example is 'If this person had done X, then the outcome would have been Y...'; 'we should have known' is closer to hindsight than to LFUO's counterfactual example.
findings.evidence: lfuo-learning-review-guide-2024-deep.md L205: 'FLA teams must guard against making counterfactual arguments such as: \'If this person had done X, then the outcome would have been Y and the accident would not have occurred.\'' [V] (Part 9, "Avoid Counterfactual Arguments"). Handout C (deep L257) supports 'interview as soon as possible'.
findings.fix: correct: LFUO's procedural responses (interview as soon as possible, Handout C; avoid counterfactual arguments such as "If this person had done X, then the outcome would have been Y", Part 9) are the direct counters.

findings.text: In retros: a close-knit team whose lead states a view early is the most exposed.
findings.problem: Superlative not supported. The source names three causes of groupthink (high cohesion, a directive leader who makes their opinions known, isolation from other viewpoints); a team with two of them is more exposed, not 'the most' exposed. The audit's own suggested wording was 'more prone'.
findings.evidence: converted L23760-23764: 'When the group is highly cohesive ... If the group leader is directive and makes his opinions known ... If the group is isolated from hearing alternative or new viewpoints, groupthink may be more likely.' Deep ref L303.
findings.fix: correct: In retros: a close-knit team whose lead states a view early carries two of the causes the source names and is more exposed.
